title: Seventy-nine days, and seventeen years after that
lede: New Coke is remembered as a product that lasted one summer. The decision lasted one summer. The drink itself stayed on shelves, under two names, until the early 2000s.

chapters.title: A lead that had been shrinking for fifteen years
chapters.cap: Coke’s share of the US soft drink market before the change, against 18.8% for Pepsi, per Beverage Digest
chapters.body:
Coca-Cola’s own account of 1985 starts with a problem: its share lead over Pepsi, “in its flagship market, with its flagship product, had been slowly slipping for 15 consecutive years.”[^1] In July 1985 UPI put the two brands at 21.7% and 18.8% of a $23-billion-a-year industry, citing Beverage Digest.[^6] Time wrote that the overall lead survived because of Coke’s strength in fountains and vending machines, and that each share point was worth about $200 million in sales.[^8]

Company officials said researchers came across the new taste in 1980 while working on a formula for Diet Coke.[^6] It was then tested on a scale few products have been: nearly 200,000 consumers over three years.[^1][^8] A spokesman gave the result as 55–45 for the new taste in blind tests, and 61–39 when tasters were told which was which.[^4]

image.caption: A New Coke can. Undated photo by Jetijonez, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.[^30]
image.alt: A red soft drink can with a silver wave, the word Coke in white and a yellow NEW! flash

chapters.title: The first change in 99 years
chapters.cap: how long the formula had gone unchanged, as reported on the day
chapters.body:
The day before, The Washington Post reported that the company “wouldn’t say what its momentous announcement will be,” and that speculation centered on a smoother, sweeter formula.[^2] On April 23 in New York, Coca-Cola “introduced the first major change in Coke’s legendary secret formula in its 99-year history.”[^3] The event was at Lincoln Center, with chairman Roberto Goizueta and president Donald Keough toasting the new drink.[^27] A later history quotes Goizueta calling it “the surest move ever made.”[^23]

The old formula was not kept as an option. Production stopped that April.[^7] Pepsi declared a company holiday.[^6] Its US president, Roger Enrico, said in a full-page advertisement that “the other guy just blinked.”[^24]

pull.text: After 87 years of going at it eyeball to eyeball, the other guy just blinked.
pull.who: Roger Enrico, president of Pepsi-Cola U.S.A., in a newspaper advertisement, as quoted by The Washington Post[^24]

chapters.title: Fifteen hundred calls a day
chapters.cap: calls a day to Coca-Cola’s hotline by June, against 400 before the change
chapters.body:
At the end of May the company asked employees to volunteer for overtime on its toll-free line. A spokesman said the reaction was “mixed.” The same day its newspaper advertisements claimed that 200 million people knew about the new taste and more than 80 million had tried it.[^4]

By June 10 the count was 1,500 calls a day, and the president of Coca-Cola USA, Brian Dyson, said most were negative. He also said 110 million people had tried the drink, that about 80% said they would buy it again, and that the company had an 18-month marketing plan, the costliest in its history.[^5] Pepsi’s advertisements said its May sales were up 14%, its best month ever.[^5]

In Seattle, Gay Mullins founded Old Cola Drinkers of America, which claimed 100,000 recruits, and sued to force the old drink back; the suit was thrown out.[^1][^6] People stockpiled. A man in San Antonio bought $1,000 worth from a bottler, and a Beverly Hills wine merchant sold 500 cases of old Coke at $30 each.[^1][^8] A Chicago research firm found that 59% of soft drink buyers who had tasted the new Coke thought the original was better.[^6]

pull.text: Does it (negative response) concern us? Absolutely. We like to please all of the people all of the time.
pull.who: Brian Dyson, president of Coca-Cola USA, UPI, Jun 10, 1985[^5]

chapters.artCaption: The hotline, 800-GET-COKE, went from 400 calls a day to 1,500.[^1] Original illustration, not an official asset.

chapters.title: “We have listened”
chapters.cap: from April 23 to the return of the original formula, as Coca-Cola counts it
chapters.body:
On Wednesday, July 10, Coca-Cola announced that it would bring the old drink back “within the next few weeks” as Coca-Cola Classic, to be sold alongside the new one.[^6] ABC’s Peter Jennings interrupted the soap opera “General Hospital” with the news.[^23] Coca-Cola stock rose $2.37 a share and PepsiCo’s fell 75 cents.[^8] Goizueta and Keough faced the press in Atlanta the next day.[^16][^18]

In the two days after the announcement the hotline took 31,600 calls.[^1] UPI reported on July 24 that the company had resumed manufacturing the original formula.[^7] Coca-Cola said the very first case would go to Mullins.[^27]

pull.text: The passion for original Coca-Cola — and that is the word for it, passion — was something that caught us by surprise.
pull.who: Donald Keough, president of Coca-Cola, at the July 11, 1985 press conference, as quoted by Snopes[^16]

chapters.title: The smaller of two Cokes
chapters.cap: share of the market left to the 1985 formula by 1999, according to one later account
chapters.body:
The two drinks got separate campaigns: “Catch the Wave” for the new taste and “Red, White and You” for Classic.[^1] Classic outsold the new formula, which by one later account settled at about a 3% share in its first year.[^16] The company did well regardless. In 1986 it reported net income up 29% to $934 million and a domestic share above 39%, which it called a record.[^11]

In March 1990 Coca-Cola said it would test the drink under a new name, Coke II.[^12] It went on sale in the Spokane area that April, with the same taste and new packaging. A brand director called it “the Coke for Pepsi drinkers.”[^13] Later accounts say the name was used more widely from 1992 and that fewer and fewer bottlers made it.[^21][^22]

The end is not well recorded. Mental Floss and The Henry Ford museum give 2002; the Associated Press wrote in 2009 that it “was sold sparingly until it was dropped in 2004.”[^19][^21][^22] In January 2009 the company began taking the word “Classic” off its labels.[^19][^20]

pull.text: It’s the Coke for Pepsi drinkers.
pull.who: Donald Lenehan, Coca-Cola group brand director for cola brands marketing, Lewiston Tribune, Apr 14, 1990[^13]

chapters.artCaption: From July 1985 there were two: the new formula, still called Coke, and the old one, called Classic.[^6] Original illustration; the lettering is ours.
